subject: Machine Learning (GATE DA syllabus section 6: Supervised + Unsupervised Learning)
weightagePercent: 11-15% of total 100 marks (~11-15 marks out of 85 core-subject marks; consistently the 2nd/3rd highest-weighted of the 7 official sections after Probability & Statistics and Programming/DSA)
difficulty: Moderate-to-High. No official IIT-published difficulty rating exists for any GATE DA edition (confirmed by the digest across all three years), but coaching-site post-exam reviews converge strongly and consistently (GeeksforGeeks, PW Live, IMS, Careers360, AspirantMitraa) on Machine Learning — together with Probability & Statistics — being the two conceptually toughest, most calculation-intensive sections every year (2024, 2025, 2026 alike). Numerically it sits in the middle: not pure-recall (like some DBMS/AI items) but generally more tractable than the hardest Linear-Algebra/SVD or multi-step hypothesis-testing questions, PROVIDED the candidate has memorized the standard formulas (entropy, Gini, sigmoid derivative, WCSS, margin, etc.) cold — most ML marks are lost to formula/arithmetic slips under time pressure, not conceptual gaps.
pyqTrendByYear: Cross-checked two independent tallies for 2025 (the prior digest's own hand-classification of the official answer key AND a fresh GeeksforGeeks "GATE DA 2025 Paper Analysis" fetch done in this session) and they agree EXACTLY: 9 questions / 14 marks (4 one-mark + 5 two-mark) in 2025. This is a rare, high-confidence data point. For 2024, the recurring coaching figure (GeeksforGeeks, MadeEasy, and the digest's own pyq_2024 entry) is 8 questions / 11 marks — consistent across sources, though (like all 2024 topic tags) it is a reverse-engineered classification, not an IISc-published number. For 2026, no primary/self-tallied figure exists yet in the digest or in what I could fetch directly; the single most-repeated secondary figure I found (Careers360's year-wise table) puts 2026 at 9 questions, ~13.85% weightage — i.e., flat versus 2025, both in question count and relative share. Net 3-year pattern: roughly flat-to-slightly-rising, 8→9→9 questions, 11→14→~13-14 marks (~11%→14%→~14% of total). One important caution surfaced during my own searches: several secondary/coaching pages (e.g., a GFG snippet and a madeeasy-derived search summary) quote a "Machine Learning 25-30% weightage" figure for both 2025 and 2026 — this is roughly double every directly-tallied count (9Q/14M ≈ 14%, not 25-30%) and is almost certainly either a copy-paste error, a stat that bundles ML+AI+overlapping-Prob/Stats content, or an unrelated generic-GATE template; I am flagging it explicitly as an outlier NOT to be trusted over the two corroborated 9Q/14M tallies for 2025.
expected2027: Medium-High confidence that ML holds at ~8-10 questions / 11-15 marks (~11-15% of total 100) in 2027 — reasoning: (1) the official 7-section syllabus text has been byte-for-byte identical for three straight years per the digest's own PDF diff, so there is no structural reason for a topic-emphasis shift; (2) the two most reliable data points available (2024's 8Q/11M, corroborated across sources, and 2025's 9Q/14M, corroborated by two independent tallies including my own fresh fetch) already show a narrow, stable band; (3) GATE DA's paper-setters rotate institutes yearly (IISc→Roorkee→Guwahati→likely IIT Madras in 2027 per the digest's syllabus_pattern entry) which introduces some setter-specific variance, so I would not claim High confidence on the exact number. Low confidence in anything above ~16-17 marks; the "25-30%" figures floating around secondary sites should NOT be extrapolated into 2027 planning without independent verification against an actual answer-key tally once the 2027 paper is released.
priorityForTopRank: High. For a time-constrained working professional targeting AIR 50-200: ML is one of the 2-3 highest-weighted subjects every year (tied with/behind only Probability & Statistics and Programming/DSA), it is entirely formula-and-numerical-technique driven (unlike AI's more qualitative search/logic content), so marks are highly "practice-recoverable" — a candidate who drills the ~14 official sub-items (regression variants, kNN, Naive Bayes, LDA, SVM, decision trees, bias-variance, CV, MLP/backprop, k-means/k-medoid, hierarchical clustering, PCA) to fluency can reliably convert 3-5 of the 8-9 ML questions into fast, low-risk marks (many are NAT/MSQ with partial-credit-free but negative-marking-free scoring). It also has high cross-subject leverage: PCA/LDA reuse Linear Algebra (eigenvalues, SVD, covariance), Naive Bayes/LDA reuse Probability & Statistics (Bayes theorem, Gaussian densities), and MLP/backprop reuses Calculus (chain rule) — so ML study time compounds with at least two other high-weightage sections. Recommended allocation: prioritize kNN, Naive Bayes, decision-tree entropy/Gini, k-means/PCA numericals first (cheap, high-frequency, low ambiguity), then SVM margin geometry and backprop (higher difficulty, still recurring), and only lastly LDA/ridge-regression nuances (lower frequency, higher difficulty-to-marks ratio).

commonMistakes: Getting bias-variance direction backwards — treating a high-bias (underfit/too-simple) model as if it were high-variance, or assuming regularization reduces bias when it actually increases bias while reducing variance
Not mean-centering / standardizing data before PCA or k-means, leading to wrong eigenvector or cluster-centroid computations
Confusing eigenvectors of the covariance matrix (correct, for PCA) with eigenvectors of the raw data matrix
Using natural log instead of log base 2 (or vice versa) in entropy/information-gain calculations — changes the numeric answer even though the concept is right
Mixing up k-means (centroid = mean, may not be an actual data point) with k-medoid (center = an actual data point, more outlier-robust) mechanics when asked to trace an iteration by hand
Confusing single-linkage (min pairwise distance, prone to chaining) with complete-linkage (max pairwise distance, compact clusters) in hierarchical clustering questions
Applying Naive Bayes without correctly using the conditional-independence assumption — computing P(features|class) as a joint probability instead of a product of per-feature conditionals
Forgetting that hard-margin SVM requires linear separability, or misidentifying which points are the support vectors (points exactly on the margin, not just 'inside' it)
Backpropagation sign/derivative errors — using the wrong derivative for sigmoid (σ(1-σ)) or ReLU (1 for x>0, 0 otherwise), or applying the chain rule in the wrong order across layers
Treating LOOCV and k-fold CV as interchangeable — LOOCV has near-zero bias but high variance and high computational cost (n model fits), which is frequently the crux of a conceptual MCQ

Burning excessive time on multi-step NAT numericals (e.g., full k-means iterations or backprop through 2+ layers) that carry no negative marking but consume disproportionate time versus their 1-2 mark value — a time-management mistake more than a content mistake
Not distinguishing supervised (labeled, predictive) vs unsupervised (unlabeled, structural) framing when a question tests only the conceptual category rather than computation
cheatSheet: Bias-Variance: High bias = underfitting (too simple, e.g. linear model on nonlinear data); High variance = overfitting (too complex, e.g. deep tree/high-degree polynomial); Regularization (ridge/lasso) trades some bias for lower variance
kNN: lazy learner, no explicit training; larger k → smoother decision boundary → higher bias, lower variance; choose k via cross-validation
Naive Bayes (MAP rule): predicted class = argmax_c [ P(c) · Π_i P(feature_i | c) ], assumes features conditionally independent given class
Logistic Regression: σ(z) = 1/(1+e^-z); decision boundary is linear in log-odds: log(p/(1-p)) = w·x + b
SVM: margin width = 2/||w||; maximize margin subject to y_i(w·x_i+b) ≥ 1 (hard margin); support vectors are the points exactly on the margin boundary
Decision Trees: Entropy H = -Σ p_i log2(p_i); Information Gain = H(parent) - Σ (|child|/|parent|)·H(child); Gini Index = 1 - Σ p_i²; lower entropy/Gini = purer split
LDA: maximizes between-class variance / within-class variance (Fisher criterion); assumes Gaussian class-conditional densities with a shared covariance matrix
k-Means: minimizes within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS) = Σ Σ ||x - centroid||²; sensitive to initialization; must fix k in advance; converges to a local optimum, not global
k-Medoid: like k-means but cluster center is an actual data point (medoid) — more robust to outliers/noise than k-means's mean-based centroid

Hierarchical Clustering: single-linkage = min inter-cluster distance (can cause chaining); complete-linkage = max inter-cluster distance (compact, balanced clusters); average-linkage = mean pairwise distance

PCA: compute covariance matrix of (mean-centered) data → its eigenvectors are the principal components, ranked by eigenvalue magnitude (= variance explained along that direction); first PC = direction of maximum variance; equivalent to SVD of the centered data matrix

Cross-Validation: LOOCV = n-fold (fit n models, near-unbiased but high-variance estimate, computationally expensive); k-fold (typically k=5 or 10) trades some bias for much lower variance and cost vs LOOCV
MLP/Backprop: gradient of loss w.r.t. each weight found via chain rule, propagated backward layer by layer; sigmoid derivative = σ(z)(1-σ(z)); ReLU derivative = 1 if z>0 else 0
Ridge Regression: loss = RSS + λ||w||²; larger λ → more shrinkage of coefficients → higher bias, lower variance, helps with multicollinearity/overfitting

Quick sanity check for classifier questions: supervised = has labeled y (regression/classification); unsupervised = no labels (clustering/dimensionality reduction) — many 1-mark conceptual questions test only this categorization
booksAndResources: Christopher Bishop, 'Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning' — most cross-source-corroborated ML textbook for GATE DA per the digest's books_resources research (named by GeeksforGeeks, DS-AI-GATE repo, Applied Course/AIR-2 blog, MathsCare, Analytics Vidhya)
Kevin Murphy, 'Machine Learning: A Probabilistic Perspective' — second most-cited ML text, good for the probabilistic framing (Naive Bayes, LDA, Bayesian view of regression)
Andrew Ng's Stanford CS229 / Coursera Machine Learning course — most-repeated lecture series across sources; strong for building intuition on gradient descent, regression variants, and bias-variance

Aurelien Geron, 'Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn, Keras & TensorFlow' — practical, code-driven reinforcement of the same algorithms (useful for intuition, not required for the theory-only GATE exam)

NPTEL 'Introduction to Machine Learning' (Prof. Balaraman Ravindran, IIT Madras, or the Sudeshna Sarkar/IIT Kharagpur version) — free, syllabus-aligned video lectures repeatedly recommended in the digest's community resource lists

StatQuest with Josh Starmer (YouTube) — not in the digest but a well-known, high-clarity resource for building fast intuition on entropy/Gini, PCA, SVM margins, bias-variance, and backprop; good for a time-constrained candidate needing quick conceptual clarity before drilling PYQs

GATE Overflow and GO Classes DA-specific ML question banks/mock tests — per the digest, these are the most-used community/coaching sources by actual DA toppers (e.g., 2025 AIR-1 Nikhil Sadineni credited GO Classes' annotated notes and mock tests)
